holding_summary: The Act of July 2, 1895 regulating and licensing public lodging houses is a valid exercise of the state's police power and does not violate constitutional requirements as to title, uniformity of taxation, or unreasonable searches. Defendant's conviction for keeping a public lodging house without a license is affirmed.

quotes.text: The whole scope and object of the act of July 2,1895, is manifestly for the preservation of the public health, the public morals and good order of society, and it is a legitimate exercise of the police power of the state, upon which there is no constitutional limitation.

During and prior to the year 1895, the defendant kept and maintained a public lodging house at 231 Crown street, in the city of Philadelphia. The defendant charged and received twenty-five cents per single night and less for each lodger.
The judgment was properly entered on the question raised by the motion in arrest, and is therefore affirmed.

holding_summary: Affirming the Superior Court, the court holds the Act of July 2, 1895 regulating and licensing public lodging houses is obviously constitutional, rejecting challenges based on the title clause, uniformity of taxation, and unreasonable searches; the conviction for keeping an unlicensed lodging house stands.

quotes.text: Robert Muir, the defendant, at the time of his arrest, kept a lodging house at 231 Crown street in the city of Philadelphia

The Act of July 2, 1895, P. L. 428, entitled “An act to regulate and license public lodging houses in the different cities in this commonwealth,” does not violate article III, see. 8, of the constitution, relating to title of acts, nor impose a license or tax lacking uniformity, nor offend against the bill of rights forbidding unreasonable searches: See Com. v. Muir, 1 Pa. Superior Ct. 578.

We have considered the provisions of the act, and are all of opinion that the Superior Court was clearly right in holding that it is constitutional. It is so obviously constitutional and valid that discussion of the subject is unnecessary.

court: Philadelphia County Court of Common Pleas
holding_summary: The 1876 Act requiring boarding houses to post rate schedules protects only boarders who relied on posted rates without their own contract; where a boarder made a special contract for room and board before occupying, entered under it, and paid under its terms without complaint, he waives the Act's protections and is estopped from invoking them against the boarding-house keeper's claim for unpaid board.

quotes.text: These two cases, although not incidental, are so similar that.the point of law raised in both of them can be considered without adverting to the difference between them. They were both actions of replevin for goods and baggage which liad been detained by certain hoarding-house keepers for non-payment of board.
it had no application to cases where the boarder, before occupying the rooms, bad made a special contract of his own.

Where a party makes his own contract, enters into possession under its terms, makes payments under its provisions, and makes no complaints as to the absence of the placards required by law, he thereby waives the benefit of the law, and is estopped from setting it up in defence of payment.

notes: The special contracts fixed a stipulated term of occupancy for the rooms, but the exact length is not given in the reported facts, so duration_of_occupancy is left unclear.

holding_summary: A landlord who boarded and lodged in a room of the house he had let to his tenants, by their permission and subordinate to their rights, was not thereby evicting them; his subsequent payment for use and occupation of the room after he ceased boarding removed any technical character of eviction, so the tenants' distress for rent was upheld.

quotes.text: This is not the case of an eviction by the landlord, of his tenants from the possession. He entered as a boarder by their permission and in subordination to? their rights. He paid for his board and lodging.
